questions.text: Why include word bounding boxes alongside recognized text in document understanding?

options.A: They prove that every recognized word is spelled correctly.
options.B: They replace the need to identify text content in the document.
options.C: They preserve spatial relationships such as columns and label-value positions.
options.D: They guarantee that every table can be converted into exact JSON.

questions.explanation: Bounding boxes retain where text occurs, helping distinguish layout-dependent relationships that plain text extraction can lose.

questions.text: Two document extractors disagree about a field. Which evidence best supports resolving the disagreement?

options.A: Choose whichever extractor emits more verbose JSON.
options.B: Inspect the source page region and retained extraction provenance.
options.C: Accept whichever answer appears first in the combined output.
options.D: Average the two values without checking the document.

questions.explanation: The original page region and extraction provenance allow the disputed value and its context to be checked against source evidence.

questions.text: The toy layoutlm_input uses text_ids=[hash(t.text)%10000 for t in tokens]. What limitation matters if these IDs are saved for later Python processes?

options.A: They are guaranteed stable vocabulary IDs across all Python processes.
options.B: Every distinct string is guaranteed to produce a distinct ID.
options.C: The IDs encode the pixel content of each image patch.
options.D: String hashes may vary across processes, and modulo reduction allows collisions.

questions.explanation: Python string hashes are randomized by default across processes; modulo10000 also allows distinct strings to share IDs. This is a toy stand-in for a tokenizer.
